beats.narration_text: Olá. This is Liam, in for Bear, with INFO 7375, Computational Skepticism for AI, at Northeastern. This film is about Gru, a persona that conducts Claude through a software design. Gru runs a design in five phases, and no phase starts until the one before it is validated. You'll watch that rule catch a component nobody asked for. The trap: a document with words in every section looks finished.

props.heading: What This Film Is About
props.question: What does Gru make you decide before Claude writes a design?

beats.narration_text: Why should you care? Ask Claude for a design and it will write a polished one, even for the wrong problem. In Gru's telling, the outage doesn't come from bad code. It comes from a decision nobody made explicitly. Vague needs upstream turn into mush in every section downstream. The gates force each decision into the open before Claude starts typing.

beats.narration_text: Four terms. An SDD: a software design document, the written record of what a system does, and why. A need: a user or business requirement that a component exists to serve. A component: a named part of the system with its own job. And falsifiable: stated so that it could turn out to be wrong.

learn.question: How does a design where every section has words fail to say why a component exists?
learn.action: Lay out the five sections, all written; drop a component into them; ask why it exists.
learn.observation: Every section is checked off, and none of them answers the question.
learn.inference: Having words in every section is not the same as having decided anything.
learn.next_question: What would a component need, to carry its own why?

beats.narration_text: Here's a design document for a checkout page. Five sections: the problem, the needs, the principles, the components, and the assembled design. Every one of them has words in it. Two months later, at two in the morning, checkout breaks inside a recommendation widget. The on-call engineer opens the document and asks one thing: why does this exist? Every section has words. None of them says why.

shot.visual_intent: Five phase squares land in a row on their spoken names (problem · needs · principles · components · SDD), each filled ink with a check mark beneath — a finished-looking document; a component dot 'recommendation widget' appears below on '2 a.m.'; the question 'why does this exist?' lands in the bottom band with a terracotta dot; caption 'constructed example'.

show.event: five squares land on their names
five check marks: every section has words
'why does this exist?' with a dot

shot.motion_claim: The five squares and the widget are the persistent objects; the question is unsolved.

learn.question: What makes a component's reason visible?
learn.action: Trace a proposed component back to a specific need from phase two.
learn.observation: The address form's line lands on the need.
learn.inference: A component that traces to a need carries its own why.
learn.next_question: What happens to a component with no need behind it?

beats.narration_text: Gru's fourth phase has one rule: every component has to trace to a need from phase two. Take the need Gru itself offers as a good one: reduce checkout abandonment caused by the three-step address form. Now propose a component, a single-page address form. Draw its line back. It lands. That component has a reason to exist, and the reason is written down.

shot.visual_intent: The checks and the widget fade; a need dot lands under phase 2 with its three-line label (reduce abandonment / caused by the 3-step / address form); a component dot 'single-page address form' lands under phase 4; an ink trace line draws from the component back to the need; a terracotta dot lands on the need; 'its reason is written down' lands in the band.
shot.motion_claim: First instance: a component whose trace lands on a specific need.

learn.question: What happens to a component with no need behind it?
learn.action: Propose the widget and try to trace it back.
learn.observation: The line stops in empty space; nothing in phase two is about recommendations.
learn.inference: The trace rule catches an orphan, as long as the needs are specific.
learn.next_question: So how did the widget get into the finished document?

beats.narration_text: Vary one thing. Someone says, we might as well add recommendations. Propose a recommendation widget, and try to draw its line back. Nothing in phase two is about recommendations. The line has nowhere to land. Gru stops right here and asks which need it serves, or calls it scope creep.

shot.visual_intent: The widget dot returns under phase 4; its trace line reaches back toward phase 2 and stops in empty space short of the need; a terracotta X at the line's loose end; 'which need does it serve?' in the band; caption 'otherwise: scope creep'.
shot.motion_claim: Second instance: the same rule, one parameter changed, and the trace has nowhere to land.

learn.question: How did the widget get into the finished document?
learn.action: Write all five sections in one pass; watch the needs come out vague; re-run the trace check.
learn.observation: With 'improve user experience' as the need, every component traces — the widget included.
learn.inference: The trace rule is only as strong as the need it lands on.
learn.next_question: What stops the needs from coming out vague?

beats.narration_text: Now the obvious approach. Skip the phases: ask Claude for the whole design in one pass, then review it at the end. All five sections fill at once, and the needs section says what first drafts often say: improve user experience. Watch what that does. The address form traces to it. So does the widget. Everything traces to a need that vague. Every check passes, and the widget ships.

shot.visual_intent: The X and the loose line clear; all five squares pulse at once; the specific need's label fades and 'improve user experience' replaces it while a pale fog grows around the need; the address form's line still lands; the widget's line now reaches into the fog and lands there too; 'every component traces. every check passes.' in the band; a terracotta dot beside the widget.

show.event: one pass: all five pulse at once
the widget's line lands in the fog

shot.motion_claim: The natural wrong turn, walked to where it breaks: a vague need is a target every trace can hit.

learn.question: What stops the needs from coming out vague?
learn.action: Put a gate in front of each phase; nothing downstream is valid until the gate before it closes.
learn.observation: The needs gate tests one thing — could the need be wrong — and the vague need fails.
learn.inference: Validation happens at the gate, before the next phase can produce anything.
learn.next_question: Once the need is specific, what happens to the widget's line?

beats.narration_text: Change the picture. Put a gate in front of every phase. Gru's rule: you cannot get a valid output from the next phase until this one has been validated. Not attempted. Not mentioned earlier in the chat. Validated. The problem passes. Now the needs gate asks its one question: could this need turn out to be wrong? Improve user experience can't be wrong. It fails the gate.

shot.visual_intent: Five open gates (thin ghost uprights) draw in front of the five squares; squares 2–5 empty to outlines and everything below dims — not yet valid; 'validated — not attempted' in the band; gate 1 closes (a thick ink upright); the band asks 'gate 2: could this need turn out wrong?'; a terracotta X under 'improve user experience'.
shot.motion_claim: The representation arrives: a gate in front of each phase, and a test the need must pass.

learn.question: Where does the widget's line land once the need is specific?
learn.action: Hold the picture; ask the viewer to commit.
learn.inference: A committed prediction turns the reveal into evidence.

beats.narration_text: Before it moves, commit. Gate two is about to force that need into something specific. When it does, where does the widget's line land? Pick your answer.

shot.visual_intent: The X clears; the band reads 'gate 2 will make the need specific'; a terracotta dot grows on the widget; the band asks 'where does the widget's line land?'; nothing else moves.

show.event: dot on the widget; the question

learn.question: What happens to the widget's line once the need is specific?
learn.action: Close gate 2: collapse the fog to the specific need, then re-run the trace at gate 4.
learn.observation: The address form still lands; the widget's line hangs in empty space and gate 4 turns it back.
learn.inference: The gate at phase two is what makes the check at phase four mean anything.

beats.narration_text: It doesn't land anywhere. The need becomes specific, and the fog it sat in collapses to one point. The address form's line finds it. The widget's line finds nothing. Gate four holds, and the widget goes back with a question instead of into the design.

shot.visual_intent: 'improve user experience' fades and the specific need's label returns; gate 2 closes and square 2 fills; the fog shrinks onto the need's single point; the address form's line brightens — still landed; the widget's line is left hanging in empty space and dims, a terracotta X at its end; gates 3 and 4 close, squares 3 and 4 fill; the widget, its line and its X slide right and fade; 'gate 4: back with a question'.

show.event: the need becomes specific; gate 2 closes
the fog collapses to a point
gates 3 and 4 close; the widget leaves

shot.motion_claim: The collision: the fog from the one-pass draft collapses under gate 2, and the same trace check now catches the widget.

learn.question: What is the general rule?
learn.action: State the gate rule over the closed chain; name what happens when a phase is skipped.
learn.observation: Every closed gate is a phase that was validated, not just attempted.
learn.inference: A phase gate: no valid output from phase N+1 until phase N is validated.
learn.next_question: Back to two in the morning.

beats.narration_text: This deserves a name. A phase gate: no valid output from the next phase until this one is validated, not just attempted. Skip one, and Gru names exactly what's missing and holds the line. Because a decision made without its prerequisite is, in Gru's words, a guess wearing a decision's clothes.

shot.visual_intent: The band clears; the title becomes 'A Phase Gate'; two rule lines land in the band — 'phase gate: no valid output from the next phase' / 'until this one is validated — not attempted' — with a terracotta dot; gate 5 closes and square 5 fills; the quote caption lands: '“a guess wearing a decision's clothes” — Gru'.

show.event: the name and the rule land

shot.motion_claim: The abstraction arrives last, as the name for the gates the viewer has been watching close.

learn.question: Why does the address form exist?
learn.action: Return to the 2 a.m. page; follow the address form's trace back.
learn.observation: The widget is absent, and the address form's why sits in phase two.
learn.inference: A gated design answers 'why does this exist?' by construction.

beats.narration_text: Back to two in the morning. Checkout breaks, but not inside a recommendation widget, because there isn't one. The engineer points at the address form and asks the same question: why does this exist? Follow the line. The answer is sitting in phase two, in words that could have turned out to be wrong.

shot.visual_intent: The rule clears; the title becomes 'Back to Two in the Morning'; a ghost ring marks where the widget would have been, captioned 'no widget: it never passed gate 4'; 'why does this exist?' in the band beside the address form; an ink dot travels the trace from the address form back to the need; a terracotta dot lands beside the need; the band answers 'the answer is in phase 2'.

show.event: a dot travels the trace to the need

shot.motion_claim: The HOOK's question returns and is answered by following the persistent trace.

learn.question: What did this leave out?
learn.action: Name the two ways around the gates.
learn.observation: Silent skips them; /claude scores at any stage without them.
learn.inference: The gates are the default; the exits are deliberate.

beats.narration_text: Two things this film didn't cover. Silent mode skips every gate, for when you already know exactly what you want and need output, not supervision. And slash claude, the boondoggle score, ignores the gates on purpose: it scores whatever exists, at any stage, across the five supervisory capacities. Neither is the default. The gates are the point.

shot.visual_intent: The need and component clear; the title becomes 'Two Deliberate Exits'; a dashed arc sweeps under the gate row from the first gate to the last — 'silent: skips every gate'; a ring of five dots — '/claude: scores what exists, any stage' with a terracotta dot; caption 'neither is the default'.

show.event: the silent arc bypasses the gates

shot.motion_claim: The boundary: the two sanctioned ways around the gates, named once each.

beats.narration_text: Let's recap with Claude. Gru conducts Claude through five phases: the problem, the needs, the principles, the components, and the assembled design. Each phase is gated: no valid output from the next phase until this one is validated, not attempted. Needs have to be falsifiable, and every component has to trace to one, or it's scope creep. And a finished-looking document proves only that every section has words.

beats.narration_text: Your turn. Paste this into Claude: Act as Gru, a phase-gated software architect. My system, in one sentence: [describe something you are building]. Run only the first two phases. First, restate my problem so that it could not describe ten other systems. Then list my needs, and reject any need that could not turn out to be wrong. Do not propose components or write any design yet. Before you run it, predict which of your needs gets rejected. Then check three things. Did it refuse to design anything before the needs were fixed? Did it reject a need you thought was fine? And could its problem statement describe ten other systems? If it could, send it back.

props.command: Act as Gru, a phase-gated software architect. My system, in one sentence: [describe something you are building]. Run only the first two phases. First, restate my problem so that it could not describe ten other systems. Then list my needs, and reject any need that could not turn out to be wrong. Do not propose components or write any design yet.
output: Check: no components, no design — until the needs are fixed.
Check: at least one need rejected as unfalsifiable.
